status_summary: A DHS memorandum dated 2025-01-20 and signed by Acting Secretary Benjamine C. Huffman superseded and rescinded, effective immediately, the 2021-10-27 guidelines on enforcement actions in or near protected areas, leaving officers to use discretion without bright-line rules; it names no categories of location. An ICE memorandum of 2025-01-31 followed, treating schools, hospitals, places of worship and sites of public demonstrations as protected areas, with case-by-case decisions by field supervisors. Courts have limited the policy only for particular plaintiffs: the District of Massachusetts on 2026-02-13 enjoined warrantless enforcement at the religious sites of eight plaintiff organizations and their member congregations (appeals pending in the First Circuit), and the Fourth Circuit on 2026-08-18 affirmed a Maryland injunction covering several Quaker, Sikh and Baptist plaintiffs (No. 25-1512). On 2026-10-20 the D.C. Circuit reversed the denial of a preliminary injunction to Mennonite Church USA and other religious groups and remanded the request (No. 25-5209) without entering one. None of these orders vacates the rescission or reaches arrests under warrants, so the rescission remains operative in general.

timeline.event: DHS issued a memorandum, signed by the Acting Secretary, that rescinds the 2021-10-27 guidelines on enforcement actions in or near protected areas and leaves officers to use discretion and common sense in place of bright-line rules; the ICE Director and CBP Commissioner may issue further guidance.

The Acting ICE Director issued a memorandum noting that the DHS memorandum of 2025-01-20 rescinded the 2021 protected areas guidelines; it treats schools, hospitals, places of worship and sites of public demonstrations as protected areas, leaves case-by-case decisions on enforcement there to assistant field office directors and assistant special agents in charge, and requires consultation with agency counsel before enforcement at a site of a public demonstration.

The District of Columbia district court denied a preliminary injunction sought by Mennonite Church USA and other religious groups, finding no showing of standing; the plaintiffs appealed (D.C. Cir. No. 25-5209).

The District of Massachusetts entered a preliminary injunction in New England Synod, Evangelical Lutheran Church in America v. DHS (No. 4:25-cv-40102) barring, absent exigent circumstances, warrantless immigration enforcement in or within 100 feet of protected religious sites of eight plaintiff organizations and their member congregations, and checkpoints aimed at people traveling to or from them; arrests and searches under administrative or judicial warrants are not restricted, the injunction controls over inconsistent parts of the 2025 policy, and the accompanying memorandum found the policy was not final agency action under the Administrative Procedure Act.
timeline.source: U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts (via CourtListener)

timeline.event: The Fourth Circuit affirmed a preliminary injunction in Philadelphia Yearly Meeting v. DHS (No. 25-1512) on Religious Freedom Restoration Act grounds; it requires DHS to follow the 2021 policy for enforcement in or near the plaintiffs' places of worship only, does not bar warrant-based arrests, and leaves in place the district court's denial of nationwide relief.
timeline.source: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit

timeline.event: A divided D.C. Circuit panel in Mennonite Church USA v. DHS (No. 25-5209) reversed the district court's denial of a preliminary injunction, holding that the plaintiffs likely have associational standing to challenge the 2025-01-20 rescission memorandum, and remanded for further consideration of the motion; the court did not itself enter an injunction (Judge Pan for the court, Judge Rao dissenting).
timeline.source: U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit

title: Rescind ICE memoranda that designate sensitive zones where enforcement is limited
uncertainties: The DHS memorandum of 2025-01-20 was read on 2026-10-26 from a copy retrieved from the official host (dhs.gov). That copy is a scanned page whose text layer has recognition errors, so its wording was checked against the copy filed as Exhibit 1 (Dkt. 1-1) to the complaint in Mennonite Church USA v. DHS, No. 1:25-cv-00403 (D.D.C.), in a RECAP mirror on archive.org, which matches it in addressees, signer, subject, date and body; the copy hosted by nafsa.org, read in earlier review, gave the same terms. The memorandum is addressed to the Acting ICE Director and the official performing the duties of the CBP Commissioner, is effective immediately, supersedes and rescinds the 2021-10-27 DHS memorandum on protected areas, and names no categories of protected location: it refers only to areas DHS previously determined require special protection and to a sensitive location. It says bright-line rules from the agency head are not necessary, says the ICE Director and CBP Commissioner may wish to issue further guidance (permissive wording, not a direction), and states that it creates no enforceable rights. The categories of houses of worship, schools and hospitals come from the 2021 guidelines and the ICE memorandum of 2025-01-31, not from the DHS memorandum. ICE's Protected Areas page on ice.gov (no date printed), read on 2026-10-26, states that the 2025-01-20 DHS directive superseded and rescinded the 2021-10-27 memorandum of the same title and describes ICE courthouse guidance of 2025-01-21; the dhs.gov page for the 2021 guidelines (last updated 2022-01-11) carries no rescission notice. The memorandum names the 2021 DHS memorandum rather than earlier ICE memoranda, so the rescission reaches older ICE sensitive-location guidance only indirectly (inference). The ICE memorandum of 2025-01-31, opened on ice.gov, recites that the 2021 guidelines were replaced, sets no fixed rules, treats schools, hospitals, places of worship and sites of public demonstrations as protected areas for ICE purposes, assigns case-by-case decisions to assistant field office directors and assistant special agents in charge, and requires consultation with agency counsel before enforcement at a site of a public demonstration. Whether that ICE-level text counts as a rescission of all ICE sensitive-zone memoranda, as the Mandate asks, or as a replacement framework is a judgment that was not resolved; no other ICE memoranda were enumerated, and no CBP follow-on guidance was found. The February 2025 date of the district court injunction in the Quaker case is from the Jurist article and was not checked against the order. On 2026-10-24 three court documents were read on court-controlled hosts: the Fourth Circuit opinion of 2026-08-18 (ca4.uscourts.gov), the D.C. Circuit opinion of 2026-10-20 (media.cadc.uscourts.gov), which also describes the 2025-01-20 rescission memorandum as issued by the Acting DHS Secretary, and the District of Massachusetts preliminary injunction of 2026-02-13 (ECF 75, read on storage.courtlistener.com); the Massachusetts memorandum (ECF 74) was read only in part on a copy hosted by courthousenews.com. The Massachusetts injunction takes effect for each protected site once a bond is posted and site lists are filed (plaintiffs filed lists on 2026-02-27 and 2026-03-06, per a Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse case summary). The CourtListener docket shows a government notice of appeal on 2026-04-14 (First Circuit No. 26-1396), a plaintiffs' cross-appeal on 2026-04-27 (No. 26-1493) and cross motions for summary judgment filed in June and July 2026; the outcome of those appeals was not found. The D.C. Circuit remanded without entering an injunction, so the Mennonite plaintiffs had no relief in place as of 2026-10-24. A nationwide vacatur of ICE courthouse-arrest policies reported in June 2026 (Sequen v. Albarran, N.D. Cal., per Bloomberg Law) concerns different policies and was not treated as affecting this record. Whether a single executive order rescinding all enforcement-limiting memoranda was issued was not checked; the rescission found is a departmental memorandum.
